_comment: The tolerance matrix, and the only copy of it. scan.py derives its skip and relax tables from this file, and the markdown table in references/context.md is rendered from it by `python3 scripts/rwlib/registers.py --write`. The matrix used to live in three places at once: prose in context.md, PROFILE_SKIP and PROFILE_RELAX in scan.py, and a test that parsed the markdown table to check the two agreed. That test was a workaround for stating the same fact twice, and it broke on table formatting rather than on a real disagreement.

_modes.strict: the rule runs at full strength. The default; rules not listed in this file are strict everywhere.
_modes.skip: the rule does not run in this register at all.
_modes.relaxed: the rule runs and reports past `allowance` hits. Relaxing is not skipping: folding one into the other is how curly-quote ended up listed in every skip set and unable to fire in any register.
_modes.partial: the vocabulary tiers drop the words carrying real technical meaning, from lexicon.json's technical_exempt. Not an allowance, which would let a second `delve` through; a named exemption list, which does not. A cell may add one further list with an `exempt` key, and technical_exempt still applies underneath it: that is how `academic` drops `paradigm` while `technical-blog` keeps flagging it, since putting those words in the shared list would exempt them in a tech blog where a new paradigm for observability is the tier-1 usage the list exists to catch.
_modes.extra-strict: flag borderline instances. A reading instruction with no mechanical form: no regex knows what borderline means.
_modes.p0-only: everything below P0 is suppressed. Implemented as a skip, because the ids it names are all P1 or P2 and the P0 fingerprints are never suppressed anywhere.

_spine_comment: `spine` is the formality ladder, loosest first, and it is the axis a document form maps onto: references/forms/*.md each name one register. Every register not on the spine is a genre column, kept because it carries tolerances no formality band captures: `technical-blog` and `docs` for the vocabulary exemption and parameter lists, `linkedin` for hashtags, bold hooks, and emoji at the end of a heading, `academic` for the vocabulary a paper needs and for the even sentence lengths a paper genuinely has. Stated as data so the split is checkable rather than a claim in a document. `casual` and `investor-email` used to sit in this list: the first collided with the voice persona of the same name, and the second was a document form posing as a strictness level, which is the whole reason forms are registers now.
_academic_comment: Every `academic` cell below was set from docs/academic-corpus/, 19 open-access papers and 72,704 words, and the ones that are not there are as informative as the ones that are. `uniform-paragraphs`, `em-dash-rate`, `rhetorical-question`, `signposting` and `hedge-stack` were all expected to need tolerances and fire on at most one paper in nineteen, so they carry no cell. `clarity` fires on 14 of 19 (`utilize`, `in terms of`, `it is important to note that`) and is deliberately left at full strength: academic writing being full of those is a fact about academic writing, not a reason to stop reporting it, and academic style guides agree.
_ste_comment: The five `ste-` rows are the mechanical band, and they run in every plain scan (`scan.py --no-ste` is the way out). Their allowances are per-document counts from three sweeps rather than from the standard: 100 trending READMEs under `docs`, this repository's own prose under `blog`, and the 19 academic papers. The advisory `ste-` ids (vocabulary, passive, modals) only run under `--ste` and carry no cells, because a tolerance on a rule nobody sees by default is a number nothing calibrates.

rules._note: Fires once per document rather than per hit, so a relaxed cell would be meaningless here: an allowance of 1 is indistinguishable from a skip. 13 of the 19 corpus papers land under the 0.45 burstiness floor. Academic sentence lengths are genuinely even, which is the register rather than a defect, and the floor is calibrated on prose that is trying not to be.
rules.label: Low burstiness

rules._note: Also once per document. 17 of 19 corpus papers exceed the 6% band. A paper repeats a construct's name for precision, and renaming it for variety is the one thing a reader must not have to do.
rules.label: Trigram repetition

rules._note: Rule 5.1, 20 words. Measured per document: 100 trending READMEs under `docs` run a median of 9 and a p75 of 19, this repository's own prose under `blog` a median of 2 and a p75 of 6, and the 19 corpus papers a median of 10. `chat`, `informal` and `linkedin` skip it outright rather than carrying a number: a word cap on a sentence is a technical-writing rule, and those three registers are not technical writing. `formal` carries no cell, which is where the rule is meant to bite.
rules.label: STE sentence length (procedural)

rules._note: Rule 6.3, 25 words. Same sweep: READMEs median 3 and p75 8, repo prose median 3 and p75 5. `academic` skips it on the same evidence that made `uniformity` a skip there: the 19 papers run a median of 52 long sentences each, about one every 75 words, which is the register rather than a defect nobody has noticed 52 times.
rules.label: STE sentence length (descriptive)

rules._note: Rule 3.4, the semicolon and the colon-joined clause. P2 throughout. `formal` and `academic` skip it because a semicolon is standard punctuation in both, which is a fact about the conventions rather than a rate: the papers still run a median of 3. READMEs median 2 and p75 9, repo prose almost none. A voice profile that rules on semicolons at all stands this down whatever the register says (scan.py).
rules.label: STE punctuation (semicolons)

rules._note: Rule 5.2, the condition before the instruction. Rare everywhere it was measured: 38 hits over 100 READMEs, 12 over this repository, and 0 in 19 papers, which is why `academic` carries no cell. `chat`, `informal` and `linkedin` skip it for the reason they skip the sentence caps: command-and-condition ordering is a technical-writing rule and those three registers are not technical writing. A register that skips three of the five and is strict on the other two is a calibration nobody chose.
rules.label: STE condition order

rules._note: Rule 6.6, six sentences to a paragraph. Counted over prose blocks only, so a ten-item bullet list is not a ten-sentence paragraph. Rare in the two markdown corpora (46 hits over 100 READMEs, 5 in this repository) and routine in the papers, median 5 and p75 10, which is what the academic allowance is set from. `linkedin` skips it with `chat` and `informal`, the same three registers that skip every other row in this band.
rules.label: STE paragraph length
